name: Anthralin (dithranol)

lead: Anthralin (dithranol) is a topical ointment mainly used for psoriasis that is also discussed for alopecia areata, the autoimmune patchy hair loss. People apply it to bald spots hoping for hair to regrow.

It irritates the skin, which is thought to shift the local immune response around the follicles, and it is reported to build up in mitochondria and slow cell division. A 2013 review reported tentative evidence of benefit for alopecia areata. It is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

paras: It comes as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%, applied to bald patches under clinician direction, often for a limited contact time before washing off. Regrowth, where it occurs, is judged over weeks to months.

Burning and irritation are reported, along with temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin and permanent staining of clothes and bathroom fixtures. In the UK it is a Pharmacy medicine, and it is used under clinician direction.

angle.text: Anthralin is a psoriasis ointment that people apply to bald spots of alopecia areata hoping for regrowth. It irritates the skin and shifts the local immune response, and a 2013 review reported tentative benefit; it is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

lead: Anthralin, also called dithranol, is a synthetic topical compound from the hydroxyanthrone family, supplied as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%. Its established medical use is plaque psoriasis.[1][2] In hair contexts it is discussed as a topical irritant treatment for patchy alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which hair falls out in round patches; people use it with the aim of regrowing hair in bald patches on the scalp, beard or brows.[1][3]

The idea behind irritant treatments such as anthralin is that mild, controlled skin irritation changes immune activity around hair follicles. A 1987 trial in 68 patients with severe alopecia areata reported a cosmetic response in 25 percent, and Wikipedia cites a 2013 review describing tentative evidence of benefit.[1][4] Pediatric and adult alopecia reviews list anthralin among available options alongside intralesional corticosteroids, minoxidil and topical immunotherapy.[3][5]
Documented effects include burning, irritation and temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin, and permanent staining of fabrics and bathroom fixtures.[1][4]

For hair, the appeal is that anthralin is one of the older topical options for stubborn patches of alopecia areata, applied directly to the bald spot in the hope of coaxing hair back, including in areas such as the beard and eyebrows where patchy loss is visible.[1][3]

paras: Anthralin is used on the skin for psoriasis. Wikipedia describes it as slower acting than topical steroids, usually taking several weeks, but without rebound flares after stopping; it is not used on the face or genitals.[1] American Academy of Dermatology guidelines on topical psoriasis therapy include it among agents with a generally high efficacy-to-safety ratio for limited disease.[2] A review of scalp psoriasis lists anthralin compounds among topical options, and a pregnancy review describes topical anthralin as among safer topical choices for localized psoriasis.[6][7]

In alopecia areata, a review chapter lists anthralin with minoxidil, topical immunotherapy and systemic immunosuppressants as options beyond intralesional corticosteroids, which it calls the treatment of choice.[5] The same chapter notes that the condition's burden is largely psychological, so treatment aims at appearance and quality of life.[5]
A pediatric alopecia areata systematic review of 122 reports covering 1,032 patients included anthralin among the treatments assessed.[3]

Reported effects include burning and irritation, which clinicians reduce by beginning with weaker preparations and increasing gradually. The compound can leave yellow-brown to purple temporary staining on skin and permanently stain clothing, shower curtains and ceramic sinks. Surrounding skin is sometimes protected with soft paraffin.[1]
In the 1987 trial every patient experienced itching and local redness with scaling.[4]

The mechanism in psoriasis is not fully understood. It is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and may generate free radicals that disrupt cellular energy and DNA replication, slowing excess cell division; anti-inflammatory effects have also been reported.[1] A 1997 review in Clinics in Dermatology covers the drug's use and properties.[8]
The Wikipedia summary adds that anthralin may lower cGMP levels and, unlike retinoids and PUVA, does not inhibit liver microsomal enzymes, so drug interactions are less likely.[1]

Anthralin appears occasionally in hair-loss discussions on T Nation, where users have posted references comparing azelaic acid and anthralin for patchy alopecia areata when discussing options for hair loss.[9][10]

Anthralin is supplied as creams, ointments and pastes from about 0.1 to 2 percent, and appears under brand names including Drithocreme, Dithrocream, Zithranol-RR, Micanol, Psorlin, Dritho-Scalp, Anthraforte, Anthranol and Anthrascalp.[1] In the UK it is a pharmacy (P) medicine, and Australia classes it as pregnancy category B2.[1]

In psoriasis practice, Wikipedia describes weaker preparations (about 0.1 to 0.5 percent) as left on overnight and stronger ones (1 to 2 percent) used for a limited period, often described as short-contact therapy, because the drug penetrates damaged skin within about 30 minutes while intact skin takes far longer; it is not used on the face or genitals.[1] Alopecia areata treatment with anthralin is an off-label dermatology use, and clinicians who use it describe starting with weaker strengths and increasing gradually to manage irritation.[1][4]

Anthralin is classed as an irritant or contact-sensitising approach to alopecia areata: the aim is to produce a mild controlled dermatitis at the bald patch that is thought to shift immune activity around the follicle. The 1987 trial in 68 patients with severe disease reported cosmetic regrowth in a quarter of participants, and every patient experienced itching and redness.[4]

A systematic review of paediatric alopecia areata treatment pooled 122 reports covering 1,032 patients, of which only two were randomized controlled trials, and listed anthralin among many options that also included corticosteroids, minoxidil, topical immunotherapy and Janus kinase inhibitors.[3] Reviews of alopecia areata describe topical irritants, minoxidil and corticosteroids as the conventional approaches for limited patchy disease.[5]
Anthralin is not an option for the common pattern hair loss that most people looking for hair regrowth have (androgenetic alopecia); it is relevant to autoimmune patchy loss.

Anthralin's ancestry is botanical. In 1876 the London dermatologist Balmanno Squire reported that Goa powder, a preparation derived from the bark of the South American araroba tree whose active compound is chrysarobin, improved psoriasis after a patient applied it to patches thought to be ringworm.[11] When natural supplies became scarce around the First World War, a synthetic compound, dithranol or anthralin, was developed, and its effectiveness in psoriasis was demonstrated in 1916.[11]

In 1953 John Ingram described how its effects could be enhanced by combining it with ultraviolet light and with adjuncts such as salicylic acid and zinc oxide, an approach that became known as the Ingram regimen.[11] Later practice moved toward short-contact preparations that are washed off after a limited time, a development used to reduce staining and irritation; its use in the United States has remained limited compared with the United Kingdom, a difference often attributed to the staining and irritation.[1][11]

sections.h: Alopecia areata and the appearance angle
paras: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, usually producing round bald patches on the scalp and sometimes affecting the beard or body hair.[12] Reference summaries put the point prevalence at about 0.1 to 0.2 percent, with a lifetime risk of roughly 1 to 2 percent, and note that in people with only one or two patches up to about 80 percent regrow hair within a year without treatment.[12] The condition does not affect body function, but hair loss can cause significant psychological distress, including loss of self-image and social anxiety.[12]

Anthralin is one of the older topical irritant treatments for patchy disease. The rationale is that a controlled mild dermatitis at the bald patch alters local immune activity around follicles.[4][1] Reference summaries list it alongside other options including corticosteroid injections, topical minoxidil, methotrexate for severe disease and, since 2022, prescription JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib, ritlecitinib and deuruxolitinib.[12]

Because natural regrowth is common, it is difficult to attribute regrowth to any treatment without a control group, a point reviewers raise about older uncontrolled series.[12][5] The pediatric systematic review lists anthralin among topical agents studied in children, and dermatology guideline summaries mention it as a lower-cost, long-established topical for limited disease.[3][5]

Forum posts that mention anthralin generally do so in passing when comparing topical options for patchy hair loss, and they do not describe it as a mainstream choice for male pattern hair loss, which is a different condition with different treatments.[9][10]

A 1987 study in Archives of Dermatology treated 68 patients with severe alopecia areata using 0.5% to 1.0% anthralin cream. All experienced itching and redness; 17 patients (25%) had a cosmetic response, 12 of whom maintained it during therapy, with mean time to response of about 11 weeks for 0.5% anthralin.[4]

Wikipedia summarises a 2013 review as showing tentative evidence of benefit in alopecia areata.[1] Systematic and narrative reviews of alopecia areata treatment include anthralin among options.[3][5] Trials of anthralin for psoriasis date to at least 1979.[13]
